messages.author: 4076f5688b45a1a5
messages.subject: plotting posterior inference on mesh
parts:
Hi! 
I have a question: i'm running a model to estimate the spatio-temporal concentration of a pollution in a certain area, starting from some known sampling stations.
I used the function inla with a matern spatial field and a autoregressive model of order 1 for the temporal residual. 
In the result object ( result <- inla(....) ) I have the element summary.random that tells me the mean of the estimation for each mesh node and for 364 days (right?).
My goal is now to plot it, possibly to have 364 plots of the pollution in the area. How can I do it? If the question is not clear please tell me I'll explain better.
Thank you very much, 
Alessandro

messages.author: afb003e064114795
messages.subject: Re: [r-inla] plotting posterior inference on mesh
parts:
Hi,
You can extract the relevant rows of the output for each time point using the information from inla.spde.make.index()
The first second or third vector (depending on how you setup the model, with group or replicate) contains the information about which elements belong to which time point.

Once you’ve done that, you have multiple options, but the inlabru ggplot() support is probably easiest. See ?inlabru::gg
Something like ggplot(result$summary.random$field[index$field.group==1,]) +
  gg(mesh, aes(fill=mean))
(I’m not at computer to check the details right now; see the help page examples that I think includes this)

Finn

messages.author: afb003e064114795
messages.subject: Re: [r-inla] plotting posterior inference on mesh
parts:
Hi,

What appears in the linear.predictor output depends on the details of
the model construction, but in general, its
(A \eta, \eta, latent)
and what's in eta and A eta depends on the inla.stack construction.
The A \eta part has the length of the number of observations, and are
the linear predictor values for the observed values, so if you only
care about that part you just need to look at those rows of the
summary.

With 49 stations and 364 days, I'd expect the first 17885 rows to be
your sought linear predictor values.
The length of eta depends on the precise inputs and options for
inla.stack(). Normally it will contain the linear predictor values for
each model component that is directly involved in the A\eta
calculation.
I'd advise against trying to extract/interpret them.

Finn
